exercises.q: Jim drove too fast, which was reckless.
exercises.why: **вёл** is the past tense (masculine) of **вести** (to lead, to preside over, to chair) — the one-direction verb of its pair, with **водить** for many directions. past: он вёл · она вела́ · оно вело́ · они вели́. — Wiktionary, «вести» (CC BY-SA 4.0).  «Unidirectional verbs describe motion in progress in one direction.» — Wikipedia, «Russian grammar» § Verbs of motion (CC BY-SA 4.0).  «to lead, to conduct — repeated function: водить — вожу, -дишь; водил; буду водить; actual function: вести — веду, -ёшь; вёл; буду вести; perfective: повести — повёл; поведу, -ёшь.» — DLI, Lesson 78.  «This verb also follows the pattern of "going verbs". Note the following meanings: 1. to lead, to take: Я веду моего сына в школу. Я каждый день вожу его в школу. 2. to drive: Кто ведёт эту машину? Он не умеет водить машину. 3. to conduct: Противник ведёт огонь. 4. to behave oneself: Этот мальчик плохо ведёт себя. Note that in the last two examples (3 and 4) only the actual function verb "вести" can be used. (Never "водить").» — DLI, Lesson 78.  Compare: «Учитель вёл школьников на экскурсию.» (The teacher was taking the children to a field trip.) — Wikipedia, «Russian grammar» § Verbs of motion (CC BY-SA 4.0). «Она водила свою подругу в театр.» (She took her friend to the theatre.) — Wikipedia, «Russian grammar» § Verbs of motion (CC BY-SA 4.0).  The other choice: **водил** is from **водить**, the many-directions verb.  ·  Sentence and translation from Tatoeba (CC BY 2.0 FR).
exercises.ru: Джим ___ слишком быстро, и это было безрассудно.
exercises.context: Unprefixed verbs of motion, which are all imperfective, divide into pairs based on the direction of the movement (uni- or multidirectional — sometimes referred to as determinate/indeterminate or definite/indefinite). (Wikipedia, «Russian grammar» § Verbs of motion (CC BY-SA 4.0))

exercises.q: Can you drive a car with manual transmission?
exercises.why: **водить** (the infinitive) (to lead, to conduct, to guide) — the many-directions (or there-and-back) verb of its pair, with **вести** for one direction. — Wiktionary, «водить» (CC BY-SA 4.0).  «Multidirectional verbs describe: 1. General motion, referring to ability or habitual motion, without reference to direction or destination; 2. Movement in various directions; 3. Repetition of completed trips; 4. In the past tense, a single completed round trip.» — Wikipedia, «Russian grammar» § Verbs of motion (CC BY-SA 4.0).  «to lead, to conduct — repeated function: водить — вожу, -дишь; водил; буду водить; actual function: вести — веду, -ёшь; вёл; буду вести; perfective: повести — повёл; поведу, -ёшь.» — DLI, Lesson 78.  «This verb also follows the pattern of "going verbs". Note the following meanings: 1. to lead, to take: Я веду моего сына в школу. Я каждый день вожу его в школу. 2. to drive: Кто ведёт эту машину? Он не умеет водить машину. 3. to conduct: Противник ведёт огонь. 4. to behave oneself: Этот мальчик плохо ведёт себя. Note that in the last two examples (3 and 4) only the actual function verb "вести" can be used. (Never "водить").» — DLI, Lesson 78.  «умеете» speaks of ability or liking — general motion, again the many-directions verb.  Compare: «Она водила свою подругу в театр.» (She took her friend to the theatre.) — Wikipedia, «Russian grammar» § Verbs of motion (CC BY-SA 4.0). «Она умеет водить машину.» (She knows how to drive a car.) — Wikipedia, «Russian grammar» § Verbs of motion (CC BY-SA 4.0).  The other choice: **вести** is from **вести**, the one-direction verb.  ·  Sentence and translation from Tatoeba (CC BY 2.0 FR).
exercises.ru: Вы умеете ___ машину с механической коробкой передач?
exercises.context: Unprefixed verbs of motion, which are all imperfective, divide into pairs based on the direction of the movement (uni- or multidirectional — sometimes referred to as determinate/indeterminate or definite/indefinite). (Wikipedia, «Russian grammar» § Verbs of motion (CC BY-SA 4.0))

exercises.q: Мы все ___ (нести — to carry on foot, one way) свой крест.
exercises.why: **несём** is the present tense (1st person plural) of **нести** (to bear, to bring, to carry) — the one-direction verb of its pair, with **носить** for many directions. present: я несу́ · ты несёшь · он несёт · мы несём · вы несёте · они несу́т. — Wiktionary, «нести» (CC BY-SA 4.0).  «Unidirectional verbs describe motion in progress in one direction.» — Wikipedia, «Russian grammar» § Verbs of motion (CC BY-SA 4.0).  «The verb "to carry" in Russian is rendered in two ways depending upon the way of carrying: on foot — носить-нести, понести; by vehicle — возить-везти, повезти.» — DLI, Lesson 78.  «to carry (on foot) — repeated function: носить — ношу, -сишь; носил; буду носить; actual function: нести — несу, -ёшь; нёс; буду нести; perfective: понести — понёс; понесу, -ёшь.» — DLI, Lesson 78.  Compare: «Она несёт домашнее задание на занятия.» (She is taking her assignment to class.) — Wikipedia, «Russian grammar» § Verbs of motion (CC BY-SA 4.0). «Он носит портфель.» (He carries a briefcase.) — Wikipedia, «Russian grammar» § Verbs of motion (CC BY-SA 4.0).  ·  Sentence and translation from Tatoeba (CC BY 2.0 FR).

Он не умеет водить машину. 3. to conduct: Противник ведёт огонь. 4. to behave oneself: Этот мальчик плохо ведёт себя. Note that in the last two examples (3 and 4) only the actual function verb "вести" can be used. (Never "водить").» — DLI, Lesson 78.  Compare: «Учитель вёл школьников на экскурсию.» (The teacher was taking the children to a field trip.) — Wikipedia, «Russian grammar» § Verbs of motion (CC BY-SA 4.0). «Она водила свою подругу в театр.» (She took her friend to the theatre.) — Wikipedia, «Russian grammar» § Verbs of motion (CC BY-SA 4.0).  ·  Sentence and translation from Tatoeba (CC BY 2.0 FR).

exercises.q: Он ___ (нести — to carry on foot, one way) сына на закорках.
exercises.why: **нёс** is the past tense (masculine) of **нести** (to bear, to bring, to carry) — the one-direction verb of its pair, with **носить** for many directions. past: он нёс · она несла́ · оно несло́ · они несли́. — Wiktionary, «нести» (CC BY-SA 4.0).  «Unidirectional verbs describe motion in progress in one direction.» — Wikipedia, «Russian grammar» § Verbs of motion (CC BY-SA 4.0).  «The verb "to carry" in Russian is rendered in two ways depending upon the way of carrying: on foot — носить-нести, понести; by vehicle — возить-везти, повезти.» — DLI, Lesson 78.  «to carry (on foot) — repeated function: носить — ношу, -сишь; носил; буду носить; actual function: нести — несу, -ёшь; нёс; буду нести; perfective: понести — понёс; понесу, -ёшь.» — DLI, Lesson 78.  Compare: «Она несёт домашнее задание на занятия.» (She is taking her assignment to class.) — Wikipedia, «Russian grammar» § Verbs of motion (CC BY-SA 4.0). «Он носит портфель.» (He carries a briefcase.) — Wikipedia, «Russian grammar» § Verbs of motion (CC BY-SA 4.0).  ·  Sentence and translation from Tatoeba (CC BY 2.0 FR).

exercises.q: Везёт тому, кто ___ (везти — to convey by vehicle, one way).
exercises.why: **везёт** is the present tense (3rd person singular) of **везти** (to convey, to carry (by vehicle), to deliver, to transport) — the one-direction verb of its pair, with **возить** for many directions. present: я везу́ · ты везёшь · он везёт · мы везём · вы везёте · они везу́т. — Wiktionary, «везти» (CC BY-SA 4.0).  Wiktionary's senses of **везти**: to convey, to carry (by vehicle), to deliver, to transport; (impersonal) to be lucky, to have luck, to work out for, to succeed, to be successful [with dative ‘for someone’ and infinitive ‘to do something’].  «The uni- and multidirectional distinction rarely figures into the metaphorical and idiomatic use of motion verbs, because such phrases typically call for one or the other verb. See below for examples.» — Wikipedia, «Russian grammar» § Verbs of motion (CC BY-SA 4.0).  «везти — Ей везёт / повезло. — She is lucky/got lucky.» — Wikipedia, «Russian grammar» § Verbs of motion (CC BY-SA 4.0).  «Note also the following idiomatic construction: Мне не везёт. — I am not lucky. Ему везёт. — He is lucky. Вам повезло. — You were lucky.» — DLI, Lesson 78.  ·  Sentence and translation from Tatoeba (CC BY 2.0 FR).
exercises.context: The uni- and multidirectional distinction rarely figures into the metaphorical and idiomatic use of motion verbs, because such phrases typically call for one or the other verb. (Wikipedia, «Russian grammar» § Verbs of motion (CC BY-SA 4.0))
